subject: Culture
title: Bastille Day
description: A quick, practical guide to Bastille Day.

hook.text: On July 14, 1789, a Paris mob stormed a prison holding just seven inmates. It changed the world.

buildup.text: The Bastille symbolized royal tyranny. Its fall became the opening act of the French Revolution.

discovery.text: France didn't officially celebrate Bastille Day until 1880—nearly a century after the event.

twist.text: The holiday actually honors a peaceful 1790 unity festival, not the violent storming. Lawmakers chose the calmer date.

climax.text: Nations pick their founding myths carefully. The symbol matters more than what actually happened.

punchline.text: The revolution began with a mostly empty prison.

quiz.question: How many prisoners were actually held in the Bastille when it was stormed?

details.summary: Bastille Day commemorates the July 14, 1789, storming of the Bastille fortress-prison in Paris — the event that ignited the French Revolution. The fortress held only seven prisoners that day, but its fall symbolized the collapse of royal tyranny and birthed modern democratic revolution.
details.whyItMatters: Bastille Day became the template for revolutionary national holidays worldwide. Its celebration shows how a single dramatic event can be mythologized into a founding story for an entire nation.
takeaways: The Bastille held only seven prisoners when it was stormed
The event symbolized the fall of absolute monarchy in France
Bastille Day became France's national holiday in 1880

faq.question: Why was the Bastille so symbolic?
faq.answer: The Bastille represented royal absolutism — a fortress where the king could imprison anyone without trial using lettres de cachet. Though it held few prisoners by 1789, it symbolized arbitrary state power. Storming it represented the people physically dismantling tyranny.

faq.question: How is Bastille Day celebrated today?
faq.answer: France celebrates with military parades (the oldest regular military parade in Europe, since 1880), fireworks, public dances (bals des pompiers at fire stations), and communal meals.
